title: Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values
subtitle: Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values: build, inspect, test, and apply the concept
description: An interactive, dashboard-focused lesson on data types, indexing and missing values, with worked code, deliberate debugging, practical transfer, and five explained application questions.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values: foundations and mental model

Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values is not just a syntax topic: it is a way to make the application’s intent explicit. Initialize descriptively named values, choose suitable types, and understand scope. A name does not itself guarantee correct storage, persistence, or display. In the Code Academy dashboard, that idea matters because Lesson attempts and scores can be analyzed with vectors and data frames while handling missing values explicitly. Start by identifying the input, the rule being applied, and the result that a learner should observe. Separate what the code declares from what it actually does at runtime. A name, selector, function, condition, or query should express one clear responsibility. When reading an example, predict its behavior before running or reviewing the output. If the prediction is wrong, trace each meaningful line instead of rewriting everything at once. This habit builds the kind of reasoning that transfers to unfamiliar code, not merely a memory of one sample. The first example introduces the smallest useful version of the idea; later examples test it against variations and edge cases.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values: Assignment binds values to names

blocks.text: Example 1 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “learner <- "Ama"”: Assigns the evaluated value to a named R object. Line 2 — “xp <- 120”: Assigns the evaluated value to a named R object. Line 3 — “cat(learner, xp, "XP\n")”: Displays the computed value so the behavior can be observed and checked. Expected behavior: Assignment binds values to names. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: Progress is stored as 4 completed lessons out of 10. Which approach avoids a stale hard-coded percentage?
options: Convert both values to formatted strings before dividing
Assume the total is always greater than zero
Calculate completed / total * 100 and handle total being zero
Store 40 separately and never update it
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Calculate completed / total * 100 and handle total being zero. A derived value should follow its source values, and the denominator must be checked.
blocks.reasoning: A derived value should follow its source values, and the denominator must be checked. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values: Inspect values and missingness explicitly

blocks.text: Example 2 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “scores <- c(4, 5, NA)”: Assigns the evaluated value to a named R object. Line 2 — “class(scores)”: Applies a summary or inspection function to the selected data. Line 3 — “is.na(scores)”: Checks missing values so the code can treat NA deliberately. Expected behavior: Inspect values and missingness explicitly. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A value represents whether a lesson is unlocked. Which type best communicates that meaning?
options: A floating-point value chosen without a defined scale
A Boolean
A display string such as "maybe"
A list containing the lesson’s entire source code
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: A Boolean. The type should express the domain meaning and limit invalid states.
blocks.reasoning: The type should express the domain meaning and limit invalid states. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values: implementation, debugging, and edge cases

Implementation quality depends on details that are easy to miss. Initialize descriptively named values, choose suitable types, and understand scope. A name does not itself guarantee correct storage, persistence, or display. Compare the expected result with the actual result, then ask which smallest change explains any difference. Check the data type, boundaries, execution order, and assumptions about missing or invalid input. For the Code Academy dashboard, Lesson attempts and scores can be analyzed with vectors and data frames while handling missing values explicitly. A solution that works only for one perfect input is incomplete. For instance, check empty strings, a zero count, an unavailable resource, an unknown key, or a repeated user action whenever those cases fit the feature. Keep responsibilities small so the cause of a defect can be isolated. The second and third examples show how to make the logic clearer and how to recognize a failure mode. Read the comments and output notes as a guide to reasoning, not as a substitute for inspecting every statement.

blocks.title: Example 3 — Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values: A list can store fields with different types
blocks.output: A list can store fields with different types.

blocks.text: Example 3 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “profile <- list(name = "Kojo", xp = 35)”: Assigns the evaluated value to a named R object. Line 2 — “profile$name”: Declares or assigns a value. The name and type determine how later expressions can use it. Expected behavior: A list can store fields with different types. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A field may be absent in downloaded JSON. What is the safest assumption?
options: Treat it as untrusted input and validate its presence and type
Assume the frontend type annotation makes the downloaded value valid
Replace every absent field with zero regardless of meaning
Read the field without a check because it exists in one test
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Treat it as untrusted input and validate its presence and type. Static annotations do not validate external data at runtime.
blocks.reasoning: Static annotations do not validate external data at runtime. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 4 — Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values: The L suffix creates an integer literal
blocks.output: The L suffix creates an integer literal.

blocks.text: Example 4 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “lessons_per_course <- 10L”: Assigns the evaluated value to a named R object. Line 2 — “typeof(lessons_per_course)”: Continues the example’s expression or control block. Read it in order with the preceding declaration and following result. Expected behavior: The L suffix creates an integer literal. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: Several functions duplicate the XP reward constant. What is the strongest improvement?
options: Copy the literal into more functions
Store the number inside an unrelated message
Make the value global and mutable without need
Use one well-named source of truth for the reward rule
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Use one well-named source of truth for the reward rule. One authoritative definition reduces inconsistent updates.
blocks.reasoning: One authoritative definition reduces inconsistent updates. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Data Types, Indexing and Missing Values: applied challenge and mastery check

Professional practice means verifying the requirement from a learner’s point of view. Initialize descriptively named values, choose suitable types, and understand scope. A name does not itself guarantee correct storage, persistence, or display. For the Code Academy dashboard, Lesson attempts and scores can be analyzed with vectors and data frames while handling missing values explicitly. Finish by following a small test sequence: verify a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case; confirm the page remains understandable; and check that the result matches the requirement rather than merely appearing plausible. Ask what would happen if one important line were removed, changed, or called in the wrong order. Distinguish a syntax error from a logic error and from an interface or data issue. The final sample brings the concept into a compact applied task, and the questions ask for decisions rather than isolated definitions. A strong answer should be supported by a reason and by a test that could prove or disprove the assumption.

Applied challenge: implement a small Code Academy feature that uses data types, indexing and missing values. Define the expected behavior in one sentence, identify the input and output, and choose the simplest code pattern above that fits. Test a normal case and an edge case. Then make one controlled change: remove a condition, alter a value, or change an input shape. Record what breaks and explain why. This is the “do and let me do” part of the lesson: the concept becomes memorable when the learner predicts a result, observes it, and explains the difference.

blocks.question: A value should never change after configuration. Which declaration best communicates that intent?
options: A formatted string that must be parsed later
A comment without any actual constraint
A constant or immutable binding supported by the language
A mutable variable reassigned repeatedly
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: A constant or immutable binding supported by the language. Use language features that express immutability instead of relying only on comments.
blocks.reasoning: Use language features that express immutability instead of relying only on comments. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: Lesson recap: Initialize descriptively named values, choose suitable types, and understand scope. A name does not itself guarantee correct storage, persistence, or display. Keep the underlying rule in mind when moving to more complex dashboard features. Syntax is the visible surface; reliable reasoning, validation, and testing are the transferable skill.
